item.description: SpaceX has launched a commercial page for Starfall, a disk-shaped reentry capsule that can carry up to 1,000 kg of payload. It can be used for manufacturing, research, or testing and is aimed at biomedical customers, pharmaceutical companies, and materials science research. Starfall's timeline will depend on Starship - SpaceX is preparing for Flight 15, where it aims to catch both stages with the launch tower.

Manufacturing in space has several advantages, one of the most important being microgravity. Varda plans to launch seven missions in 2027 and 10 in 2028.

item.title: How software engineering is changing: a tale of two eras (32 minute read)
item.description: AI-native startups can ship even faster than fast-moving pre-AI startups because they risk nothing by moving too fast. The old constraints of software engineering have disappeared, allowing startups to move faster, but also break things. The new constraints are too much context switching, losing shared context, tougher pacing, less focus on design, and AI plan limits. Many existing technologies and processes will crack under the change.

item.title: Interpolative Software (5 minute read)
item.description: Interpolative software is code that is solidly within the training distribution of models. It can often be specified with just a few sentences of prompting. Novel software is something that has fundamentally not existed before. Writing novel software with agents is challenging, as they are not trained on the task. Not a lot of software is novel, which is fine, as there is still a ton of value in the interpolative stuff.

item.title: The Death of the Angel Investor (6 minute read)

Also, when angels try to fund a round, they are often pushed out by the valuation game.

item.title: What Is Quantum Advantage Actually Worth? (9 minute read)
item.description: Nearly all roadmaps point to a utility-scale quantum computer being developed around 2030. Despite this, there is little confidence or clarity on how these machines will actually be useful. The consensus is now that they'll first be used for breaking cryptography. The second most concrete answer is to use them to generate simulation data for AI labs' science models. This post looks at how else quantum computing could be applied and where all the revenue will come from.

item.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI (31 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI's monorepo's size and demands increased at a staggering pace over the last year, necessitating a revamp of the AI lab's source control system. Its technical staff built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches and to maximize read throughput. The team implemented the backend without interrupting any engineering work or changing how the team uses Git. Pando cut median push latency in production by nearly 5x, and it now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

item.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
item.description: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

item.title: The value of open source (16 minute read)
item.description: People open source projects for various reasons. Some do it to build a company or product, others do it performatively, and some ship code just for the love of the game. Open source was never free to copy, and the code was never the moat. AI can remake a product, but it can't provide the rest of the value a company generates. The technology is helping maintainers ship and fix problems faster.

item.title: Our organizations are being DDoSed from the inside (6 minute read)
item.description: Organizations are losing attention as everyone within is doing something they think is useful, but all that work draws on the same limited capacity to understand, review, and decide. Just because work exists doesn't mean it's the right thing to do. Output is not proof of value. A working implementation only means that something can be built, not that it should be - some changes have negative value.

item.title: Making agents fast - what I've learnt over the last 12 months (12 minute read)

item.title: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display (2 minute read)
item.description: The new MacBook Pro has an OLED touchscreen display. The display can achieve 2,000 nits of maximum brightness, and Apple claims it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The new laptop is lighter than the previous model at just 3 pounds. The top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a Dynamic Island, and the Apple logo on the back of the lid glows like in older models.

item.title: Google unveils Gemini 4 Carbon, retaking the world's no. 1 spot on updated, harder benchmarks — but access is limited (17 minute read)
item.description: Gemini 4 Carbon promises improvements in cybersecurity and complex software engineering. It is now available to selected cybersecurity defenders. A broader release will be available after Google improves guardrails on the model based on feedback. Carbon will launch at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a 95% discount for cached inputs. Prices will return to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens when the introductory period ends.

item.title: The last, best hope for space tourism just rolled onto a runway in Arizona (2 minute read)
item.description: Apeiron, a Delta-class suborbital spacecraft from Virgin Galactic, is being moved from Virgin Galactic's Spaceship Factory in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico. After its arrival, aircraft engineers and technicians will complete work on the vehicle's avionics equipment and flight software. Apeiron will still require several ground tests and test flights before it can make a free flight. Virgin Galactic expects Apeiron's first commercial spaceflight to take place early in the second quarter of 2027.

item.title: Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen (3 minute read)
item.description: The Grid is a factory-scale robot that can build circuit boards on demand. Every board takes its own route through the factory, which has machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder, and inspect. With The Grid, printing one unit of 100 designs is as easy as printing 100 units of one, and prototypes and production batches run on the same machines. It allows companies to manufacture huge numbers of low-volume boards, and could help bring manufacturing back to the US.

item.title: Introducing the Slack Code API: Your agents, your team, one code channel (6 minute read)
item.description: The Slack Code API allows agents to start code channels, add relevant people and files, post updates as they work, and archive channels when the work is done. It enables teams to work together with agents on tasks with the same shared context. Users can see exactly what agents are doing and who approved it, and workspace controls and data boundaries are built in. Users can choose what agents and models they want to use to suit their needs.

item.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development (13 minute read)
item.description: Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for a while, but the games weren't fun. The latest generation of models exhibit meaningful improvements in game design, allowing them to create games with novel, compelling gameplay loops. The challenge now is coming up with concepts for games that wouldn't exist without AI assistance.

item.title: The Sane Asylum (32 minute read)
item.description: It is now possible to build a highly profitable business with significant scale without raising or hiring a ton. Founders can take advantage of new AI tools to generate financial freedom and build organizations to work on the things they want to, with the people they want, at a scale, ambition, and pace that works for them. This article explores how the founders of turbopuffer, a startup that powers the search infrastructure for many AI companies, built their company. It explores what life and work in the time of AI can look like, and shows how ambitious builders and founders can try it for themselves.

item.title: Google Shares Fall 10% as Growth in Search Revenue Slows (5 minute read)
item.description: Google's advertising business failed to deliver on analysts' estimates in the third quarter. The company is still figuring out how to translate AI into faster sales in its core web-search business. While Alphabet reported 25% revenue for the quarter, revenue from search advertising decelerated. Its cloud business exceeded analyst expectations, drawing in $30.7 billion out of Alphabet's total of $127.6 billion in sales.

item.title: Apple refreshes the iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip (2 minute read)
item.description: The iMac and the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro are both getting the M6 chip. The iMac will have two variants of the M6 chip, one with a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, while the other will have 12 cores for each. The MacBook Pro will only have the 12-core option. Both computers will have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity, which means they will have Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Pre-orders will start on October 28, and they will start shipping on November 6.

item.title: Anthropic Raises Concerns (21 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic's prospectus claims the biggest risks to its business are risks the business poses to everyone else. All other human enterprise will be eaten by Claude, so you might as well own some of it. The company's governance structure is exactly what you would expect for a company worried about existential AI risks. However, it is also the same governance structure for a startup that wants to raise a lot of outside capital without losing control.

item.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software (13 minute read)
item.description: Researchers based in China have collaborated to create a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with specified functions. This could enable anyone to design proteins - if they have a lab that can sort the good designs from the failures. The model's success rate is not great, but it can still get the job done. The tool likely won't remove the need for biologists, but it could help accelerate research.

item.title: Sunlight at night: US startup's demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticism (6 minute read)
item.description: Reflect Orbital is a US-based startup that plans to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight onto the Earth during night-time. The Federal Communications Commission has approved the startup's proposal to launch an initial demonstration satellite next year. The test will reflect sunlight in 3-mile-wide beams in strengths from moonlight up to the brightness of the Sun at noon. While the technology could be helpful for search-and-rescue operations, among other applications, critics say that it threatens a harmful change to the separation of night and day, with a huge number of unresolved questions and significant potential impacts.

item.title: Hunger beats tenure: Advice for junior engineers (5 minute read)
item.description: The coding interview was never popular, and AI is likely going to make it go away for good. Impact is now less bounded by years of accumulated knowledge. Fresh eyes have long been considered powerful, as newcomers often see things old-timers miss. Look for candidates with prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking.

item.title: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI (4 minute read)
item.description: Amazon has released a memo to staff saying that token usage and code generation should be considered with care and judgment. The company has not instituted caps on employees' token usage, but it has acknowledged that metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain deeply flawed ways of measuring AI usage, and that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity. The company is now looking at how many launches it is doing and how many successful changes it is making in production to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.

item.title: DoorDash Is in Advanced Talks to Acquire Delivery Rival Instacart (2 minute read)
item.description: DoorDash is looking to acquire rival Instacart in a deal that would value Instacart at around $17 billion. The deal could be finalized as soon as this week, but there is no guarantee it will come together. Instacart's core business involves online grocery shopping and convenience home delivery from retailers. The acquisition will add to DoorDash's food delivery services from retailers such as Kroger, Safeway, and Aldi.

item.title: The Biggest Takeaways From Anthropic's IPO Prospectus (8 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic unveiled its IPO paperwork yesterday, putting it on track to go public as soon as the week before Thanksgiving. The 400-page prospectus tells a story of how the company could usher in a new era of progress that will transform how people code, conduct research, build financial models, and automate routine tasks. It also warned that AI could lead to the development of new bioweapons, destabilize the geopolitical order, and evolve beyond the ability of humans to understand and control. Anthropic plans to trade on the NASDAQ under the ticker 'ANT', with a valuation expected to land between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

item.title: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding (12 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI has announced three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics. For the math result, which is about harmonic analysis, the AI lab will release the AI output, so researchers are free to organize their own efforts to explain the result. OpenAI will form an external group of collaborators to explain the computer science result, which is about complexity theory, and will make the AI output publicly available. The lab will also form an external group of collaborators for the physics result, which is about quantum field theory, but defer to them on the release of the materials.

item.title: 'It's offensively cheap': How solar power is quietly becoming bigger than nuclear (9 minute read)
item.description: Solar power will likely provide 10% of the world's power by the end of the year. Solar electricity is the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history as it has become unbelievably cheap. China is still the world's biggest solar power producer by far, but the installations in the US are skyrocketing. Even with tariffs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US, and it is getting built regardless of political lines.

item.title: The Counting House (49 minute read)
item.description: The Counting House pattern adds AI to systems that handle large volumes of human work, notably customer service departments. It can be used to control and improve costs, quality, and human ramp-up time using comparatively cheap AI models. A Counting House uses classic data science and engineering to put lower-tier models on hardened rails to support human workflows. It allows teams to measure and report how well models do against their human counterparts.

item.title: How the Claude Code team does code review (18 minute read)
item.description: Claude writes about 90% of the code in Claude Code. This post explains how the team reviews the code at the volume its agents produce. The team moved most of the reading in the review stage to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. This resulted in merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubling while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40% between June and September.

item.title: Microsoft Will Offer Buyouts to 60,000 Employees (3 minute read)
item.description: Microsoft is extending voluntary buyout offers to 60,000 employees in Canada, India, the UK, and the US. The program is time-limited. It provides eligible employees with financial support and career planning services. Microsoft expects less than 30% of employees will accept the latest buyouts. The voluntary retirement program is part of a broader shift by Microsoft to alter its performance system and how it awards bonuses and stock options.

item.title: The End of the Internet (18 minute read)
item.description: Blogging began to die when Google started aggregating the internet. Social media made it much easier to create and share content, but this caused the amount of content to increase by orders of magnitude. Algorithms started to matter, and then these sites started becoming personal entertainment sites, tuned for engagement. The latest series of security vulnerabilities unveiled by AI will further shrink the public internet.
